title: Mumbai's dabbawalas: how the lunch-box delivery system works

sources.title: Mumbai's dabbawalas still serving up lessons in lunch (2008-11-11)

facts.text: Dabbawalas pick up home-cooked lunches in metal boxes from homes in Mumbai and deliver them to office workers.
The lunch delivery service has run since 1890.
Around 5,000 dabbawalas deliver about 200,000 lunches a day (reported in 2008 and again in 2021).
Boxes are carried to the nearest railway station, sorted, loaded onto crates, and taken by commuter train toward the offices.
Dabbawalas move the boxes by bicycle, on hand carts, or on long trays balanced on their heads.
A box usually changes hands several times on its way from a home to an office.
After lunch, the empty boxes are collected from offices and returned to the customers' homes.
Many dabbawalas have had little formal schooling, so boxes are identified by colors and, later, letters and numbers rather than written addresses.
Business schools have studied the system, which is reported to make very few mistakes.
Before the first delivery for a new customer, a dabbawala visits the home and the office to learn the way.
Dabbawalas work through monsoon rains and heat, and they plan around frequent train delays to deliver on time.
Money earned by a group of dabbawalas is shared equally among its members.
Many dabbawalas followed their fathers into the job.
Food delivery apps have made it harder for dabbawalas to find customers.
